deep.reconstruction:
This page has no mathematics. It is part of a German prose narrative of ancient history, apparently lecture notes. It continues the previous page on Alexander's Indian campaign and return through Gedrosia, and ends the 'first period' just before the next page opens 'Zweiter Zeitraum. Von dem Tode Alexanders M. bis auf die Schlacht bei Ipsus, 323–301'.

Content, paraphrased:
(1) Nearchus, with the fleet, and Alexander arrived safely at Babylon, dated 325.
(2) From there Alexander planned or undertook an expedition into the northern lands and to Arabia, in order to conquer it.
(3) Babylon now became his residence.
(4) He married the daughter of Darius, and all the nobles had to do the same.
(5) He adopted Persian customs and promoted trade.
(6) At Babylon he had a harbour built that could hold 1000 ships, and he had the canals cleaned.
(7) He died in 323, on 21 April, in the 33rd year of his age and the 13th of his reign.

There are no derivations, formulas, computations or numerical methods to reconstruct. The only numbers are historical dates (325, 323), a ship count (1000) and ages or regnal years (33, 13). The handwriting and genre (a world-history course divided into 'Zeiträume') suggest student or lecture notes on ancient history. They are probably not Gauss's own mathematical work, and possibly not in his hand at all.
errors: Chronology: Nearchus met Alexander again in Carmania and Susa in 324 BC. Alexander did not settle in Babylon until spring 323 BC, so 'Babylon 325' is early. 325 BC is the year of the Gedrosian march.

The marriage to Stateira, daughter of Darius III, and the mass weddings of the Macedonian nobles with Persian women took place at Susa in 324 BC, not at Babylon. The page does not state the place explicitly, but the context implies Babylon.

Date of death: modern scholarship places Alexander's death on 10/11 June 323 BC (from the Babylonian astronomical diary). '21 April' does not match this; it may reflect an older conversion of the Macedonian date (28 Daisios).
Alexander was 32 years old, i.e. in his 33rd year, which is consistent. His reign ran from 336 to 323 BC, about 12 years 8 months, so 'the 13th year of his reign' is consistent.

results.what: Historical narrative of Alexander the Great's final years: return to Babylon, the planned Arabian expedition, the Susa marriages, adoption of Persian customs, the harbour for 1000 ships at Babylon, canal clearing, and death in 323 BC.
results.modern_name: Ancient history (Alexander the Great, after Arrian, Anabasis Book 7)
results.usually_credited_to: Arrian, Diodorus, Plutarch as ancient sources; contemporary textbook or lecture tradition (e.g. Göttingen history courses such as Heeren's)

deep.surprise_reason: The page is non-mathematical standard ancient-history lecture material, probably notes taken by a student or family member. It has no bearing on Gauss's mathematics.

checkable.asserts: The 'second period' heading on the next page (323 to 301 BC, Alexander's death to Ipsus) spans 22 years.
The reign counted by year numbers from 336 BC to 323 BC reaches 13, consistent with 'the 13th year of his reign'.

transcription_corrections: Line 1: '[?] Brech[?]' should read 'Nearch' (Nearchus), i.e. 'So kam Nearch und Alexander glücklich nach Babylon 325.' The first word is likely 'So' rather than 'Er'.

Line 2: 'unternahm[?]' is uncertain; the image may read 'wollte er eine Expedition … machen'. The verb is unclear, and the following 'und um es zu erobern' suggests a planned rather than completed expedition.
